data.fundamental-principles-of-system-archite:
A dense and to-the-point article about the underlying fundamentals of System Architecture.
July 2026 · 17 min read

data.architecture-for-a-system-lifetime#Archi:
For a large, long-lived system, technologies may change, teams may come and go, components may be outsourced, but the system persists. The system at the end of its life may be very different from its first iteration.
The larger a system is and the more changes it is expected to go through in its lifetime, the more critical it is to understand and apply the principles laid out in this article.
Meaningful grouping into components is essential. Think of coupling and cohesion as heuristics for a grouping algorithm, qualitative in nature, designed to help mitigate our human limitations. Effective grouping requires a deep understanding of the domain and the actual dependencies within the system.
Knowing the interfaces is key for any component- or service-oriented architecture because they define the requirements for components and establish responsibility boundaries between teams.
Knowing how the system fits together, understanding the composition, is equally important. A composition can range from a simple drawing to the use of a dependency injection framework to the automatic deployment of an entire system with orchestration.
It is also critical to establish an interface specification inventory with good governance. Changes to interface specifications need to be agreed upon, documented, and communicated to prevent integration issues. Both the client and server sides are equal stakeholders, but in my experience, it works best if the server side holds the pen.
At their core, both the composition and the interface inventory are forms of communication. With a good handle on these:
We can evolve the system step by step in a controlled, non-disruptive way through clever use of backward compatibility. We can reuse components for other projects. We can substitute components to support different needs in functionality and cost, for example by swapping in (or out) a COTS product to save time and money. We can introduce variability in the composition on top of a common base of components, creating variants that serve different users’ needs—a cost-effective product line.
data.branching#Branching:
Some users value new functionality, while others prioritise stability. Unfortunately, there is an inherent conflict between quality and new functionality because adding new features often introduces defects.
As new functionality is constantly added, the quality often suffers. By focusing solely on bug fixes, security patches, and support for new 3rd party product versions, the quality increases monotonically for a release.
This type of policy is relatively common and offers users a choice:
either run with the latest and accept the risk of poor quality, or lay back and ride in comfort of stability. However, fixing bugs found in older releases requires mapping them to newer releases, as users upgrading don’t want to encounter the same old bugs. This process is tedious, error-prone, and time-consuming. The effort grows with a lack of initial quality and the number of supported releases. Many companies limit the number of supported releases by implementing an end-of-life policy that compels users to upgrade.
Interface specifications typically follow a more lightweight branching pattern. One school of thought is that specifications, by definition, don’t have bugs, so there are no patch releases.
data.coupling-and-cohesion#Coupling and Cohes:
Coupling and cohesion are about managing complexity by grouping code that is highly interdependent, while at the same time having as few dependencies between the groups as possible.
When a group has only code that is highly interdependent cohesion is high, and when there are few dependencies between groups, coupling is low.
Errors and changes manifest along these lines of dependencies. Problem-solving is faster and easier when problems are subdivided, and also humans understand by grouping things.
In their 1974 paper “Structured Design” Stevens, Myers, and Constantine emphasise that coupling and cohesion are at odds, and that there is a sweet spot in between.
Try to minimise coupling, and the groups become larger, but now with heaps of superficially related code. This does not aid problem-solving.
Try to maximise cohesion, and the groups become smaller, but with more interdependencies until there is effectively no subdivision anymore—also not aiding problem-solving.
Finding the right balance takes practice and refactoring, a lot of refactoring.
In short, coupling and cohesion lead to grouping of code in a way that facilitates problem-solving and understanding.
data.dependency-direction#Dependency Directio:
Dependencies often have a direction, meaning that it is optional on one side, both syntactically and semantically. For example, in SW calling a function may be optional and for a HW connector a pin may be optional on the male side.
When all underlying dependencies have the same direction, the interface has that direction too. Based on the directions of the interfaces, it is possible to re-arrange the visualisation into a directed graph, with the general direction pointing down and composition vertical.
The visualisation quickly becomes busy unless interfaces are hidden and it is often preferred to use two views: the view to the left puts more emphasis on the importance of interfaces and reuse, while the one to the right puts more emphasis on how the system is organised.
If you are working in software, you might recognise this under the name ‘dependency inversion’. Personally I find this name misleading - this was always the natural way dependencies are organised - we just lost our ways for a while.
Having acyclic dependencies is beneficial because quality will tend to stabilise quicker after a change or bug-fix. Personally I find it is easier to grasp a system with acyclic dependencies.
data.early-vs-late-binding#Early vs. Late Bin:
The composition specifies which components are used in a system. Somehow the components must be hooked up so that information can be shared across the interfaces. This is referred to as binding.
When designing a system, it is also crucial to consider binding time — that is, when the components are bound together — because there are significant trade-offs to be made.
Early or static binding, during compilation or linking, gives good performance as there is no look-up logic required in calls between components. However, it offers no flexibility to swap components once built.
Late or dynamic binding offers more flexibility to upgrade individual components. However, comes with more complicated distribution and the risk of dependency hell.
Networked or configurable binding, such as REST API, offers flexibility for distribution, scaling and upgrading parts on the fly. However, adds communication and configuration overhead.
The ability to re-bind in run-time is impressive but non-trivial to implement. USB devices manage surprisingly well most of the time.
Note that late binding will not, on its own, lower coupling, as the number and nature of dependencies are determined by the interfaces.
data.interfaces#Interfaces:
An interface is a shared boundary across which two or more components exchange information. To exchange information means there is a dependency. An interface embodies a set of dependencies.
Because interfaces provide this abstraction, the embodiment of dependencies, it is possible to substitute any of the components for another as long as it complies with the interface.
And, the developers of component A can develop to the interface without knowing anything about the implementation of B; all the nitty gritty details of component B are abstracted away by the interface.
An interface inherently exists between connected components. There may or may not be a specification - many interfaces are undocumented or schema-less.
Now, the most important insight related to interfaces is this:
component A depends on the interface (and not on B) and at the same time component B depends on the interface (and not on A) The interface itself does not depend on components A or B at all!
We illustrate this by drawing the interface below the components.
data.multiple-teams-and-scale#Multiple Teams:
The emerging pattern that comes from coupling and cohesion is recursive and repeats itself at different scales:
functions are grouped into modules or classes modules or classes into libraries or systems systems are grouped into larger systems At each level, it’s important for coupling to be low between groups and cohesion to be high within groups. From this point onwards, I will refer to a group of code as a component. Please keep in mind that different constructs are used at various scales.
Humans are social beings and tend to work best in teams of around 3 to 7 people. At a certain scale, a team is typically assigned to develop and maintain a component. Members of one team must trust that other teams do not alter the nature of dependencies in an uncontrolled manner.
A software contract can be seen as an interface specification combined with an agreement on when and how changes are permitted. This leads us to the most super-hero concept in engineering: the interface.
data.the-natural-order-of-dependencies#The Na:
For a real system there must also be something that knows about which implementation is used where. I will refer to this as composition.
So there are effectively three levels:
interfaces components composition Having composition separate from components enables substitution. It can improve cohesion, but note that it does not on its own lower coupling as the number and nature of dependencies are determined by the interfaces.
Reuse is enabled by well designed interfaces, which also imply low coupling.
This emergent pattern arguably represents the natural order of dependencies for any system composed of components. It is there for us to recognise, rediscover, and align our designs to.
Back when I was a junior developer, a senior colleague tried to teach this pattern to me. After explaining patiently for hours he exclaimed: “Andreas, if you don’t understand this, it is your problem.”
He was right.
data.the-problem-system-architecture-solves#T:
You know the story: users keep pulling your system in different directions. Some want new functionality. Others want different functionality. Some just want stability.
Every large system that needs to keep changing eventually runs into the same problem: how do we change one part without breaking another?
Dependencies make the system too complex for one person. Teams help, but humans do not coordinate too easily in large groups.
Over time, engineers have developed a set of core principles to manage this:
coupling and cohesion interfaces composition branching compatibility These principles are not arbitrary. This article traces how they emerge from the problem itself, and why they appear again and again across engineering disciplines.
data.version-variant-and-compatibility#Versio:
Not only do different users put different value on stability versus new functionality, they also value different functionality in different packaging.
The difference between a version and a variant is that newer versions eventually replace earlier ones, while variants are designed to live side by side.
The key to cost-effective variants is building them from a common base of components. Variability can be controlled by altering the composition or by unlocking features with configuration hidden from the user.
Deciding whether to maintain compatibility across versions is an important, and often difficult, decision:
For larger systems, where each component is version-controlled and perhaps released separately, breaking compatibility can be a major headache: only certain version ranges will work together, and users can end up in dependency hell. On the other hand, if compatibility is never broken, the product will eventually stagnate. An implementation is backward-compatible when it supports all dependencies that the previous release did, both syntactically and semantically.
An interface specification is backward-compatible when it is a superset of the previous version, with added dependencies marked as optional.
data.why-dependencies-make-engineering-hard#W:
Why are systems so expensive to create? And, what is software anyway?
Software is information—instructions to a computer. For the purpose of this series, we’ll consider software as created by a human and expressed in a formal language such as C, Java, or Python.
What makes software challenging is the abundance of dependencies. A dependency occurs wherever one piece of code relies on another for its proper operation. For example, when a function calls another function, or when a member in a struct is referenced.
And there are a lot of dependencies.
Errors and changes manifest along these lines of dependencies. Introducing a modification can easily lead to an error if not all dependencies are taken into account. As these dependencies cascade, the task becomes increasingly challenging for larger systems.
This challenge is not unique to software engineering; other fields, like Electrical Engineering, also grapple with numerous dependencies. Mitigating includes prototyping and testing which is time-consuming and therefor expensive.
data.why-these-principles-are-fundamental#Why:
In this article we have explored a number of principles, but what is it that makes them fundamental?
It’s because they stem from 3 universal needs:
complexity must be managed because as humans we have a limited capacity, as humans we tend to work best in small teams, and users have different preferences. For larger systems with a high number of dependencies the pattern that emerges from cohesion and coupling becomes almost a natural law due to statistical properties, enabling us to manage complexity.
Interfaces enable us to manage dependencies and decouple complex problems into components that can be worked on by individuals or teams.
Branching and backward compatibility are a direct response to different users having different needs for functionality and stability.
All of these principles show up time and time again, across different scale, and across different technologies. In contrast, evolution seems to have little need for this type of concepts. If (or when) super-human intelligence ever becomes a thing, it will be very interesting to see how it organises what we know as software.
But for now, there you have it: fundamental principles of system architecture.
Andreas Olsson

data.how-to-best-organise-your-code---balanci:
What if there is a conflict between coupling / cohesion and common sense?
April 2024 · 2 min read

data:
In the realm of system design, the key limitation we face is our human cognitive capacity. We have a finite ability to comprehend and manage complexity.
To effectively manage complexity, we must organise systems into manageable components - be it classes, functions or modules, or larger parts.
There are many principles that can help guide how to group these components, but in my personal experience I have found two that stand above the rest: coupling and cohesion, and cognitive coherence.
Coupling and Cohesion: These concepts revolve around the idea of modularity. Coupling measures the strength of relationships between components, while cohesion quantifies the degree to which elements within a component are related or serve a common purpose. These principles help us create modular, maintainable systems by balancing interdependence and internal consistency.
Cognitive Coherence: This concept focuses on communication, both with others and with our future selves. Achieving cognitive coherence means designing systems that are intuitively understandable. It involves ensuring that the structure and organisation of the software align with our cognitive processes, facilitating comprehension and decision-making.
Both coupling and cohesion, and conceptual coherence are vital principles in software design, guiding the creation of modular, maintainable, and understandable systems.
But what if there is a conflict? If these principles pull in different directions?
Conflict between Cohesion and Conceptual Coherence: Sometimes, improving conceptual coherence may necessitate sacrificing cohesion. For example, consider the standard library header file math.h. While it provides a diverse range of mathematical functions, its cohesion may suffer due to the broad scope of functionality it encompasses. However, sacrificing cohesion in favour of improved conceptual coherence can still be justified if it enhances overall system understanding and usability.
High Coupling and Conceptual Model Mismatch: High coupling can indicate a mismatch between the conceptual model and the system’s requirements. In my personal experience, encountering high coupling has often been a sign that my conceptual model was flawed. For instance, when designing a complex system, if the components exhibit excessive interdependencies, it may be time to reassess the underlying conceptual model to better align with the system’s needs.
While there may be instances where one must be prioritised over another, I strongly believe we can, and should, use both these principles and create systems that are not only modular and maintainable but also conceptually coherent and intuitively understandable.
Andreas Olsson

data:
Business architecture often describes what the enterprise wants. System architecture explains how responsibility is decomposed, allocated, integrated, verified, and proven. High-security and high-compliance environments require both.
I have my roots in systems engineering. Large systems. Complex problems. No well-established industry patterns for breaking the problem into manageable chunks. I learned that interfaces and software contracts are fundamental to enabling teams of engineers to work independently, side by side.
Business architecture comes from another tradition. It solves a different set of challenges. Enterprise, domain and solution architects usually have the luxury of focusing on business value, processes and data because many technical interfaces are already defined by standards bodies or suppliers. Integration is often considered afterwards, with a focus on data models.
But high-security and high-compliance environments are much less forgiving.
My concern here is with business-oriented architecture in enterprise IT, particularly when its models are not complemented by explicit interface specifications and deliberate allocation of security requirements across subsystems.
data.conclusions#Conclusions:
High security and high compliance expose the gap between stating what the enterprise must achieve and demonstrating how its requirements are fulfilled.
Business architecture remains essential. It provides the purpose, priorities and organisational context needed to make sensible engineering decisions. System architecture brings the discipline to translate those decisions into obligations that can be assigned, integrated and verified.
Interface specifications belong at the centre of that collaboration. Standards and suppliers may define how systems communicate, but the organisation must still establish what each side guarantees and how those guarantees fulfil the wider requirements. Interfaces must be treated as contracts to design and verify.
Explicit interface contracts also allow teams to develop and verify their own parts independently, with a clear understanding of what they must provide and what they can rely on from others.
High-assurance organisations need architects who can connect the enterprise view with these system-level responsibilities. The architecture must show not only that the individual parts meet their obligations, but that those obligations fit together to fulfil both the business and the security requirements of the whole.
Andreas Olsson
data.how-system-architecture-comes-to-the-res:
System architecture starts by defining the system boundary, its dependencies and its interactions with other systems and actors. It then decomposes the system and allocates requirements deliberately. The same discipline applies at each level, from the system of systems down to its subsystems, including the people, processes and suppliers needed to fulfil the requirements.
Interface specifications make the responsibilities at each boundary contractual. They define what each side must provide, what it may assume about the other and how failures are handled. Security obligations, operational ownership and evidence requirements belong alongside protocols and data formats. The interface becomes an architectural object to design, maintain and verify, not merely a connection to implement.
Requirements can then be traced from their source through their allocation to the relevant interfaces, verification methods and evidence. Each subsystem can be assessed against its own obligations, and handovers can be verified against agreed contracts. Requirements concerning the combined behaviour of several subsystems must still be verified at the system level. Decomposition makes verification manageable; it does not remove responsibility for the whole.
Evidence is planned as part of this work. The architecture identifies what must be demonstrated, where the evidence is generated, who owns it and how it is protected and retained. Verification and audit then have a defined chain to follow, rather than one to reconstruct afterwards.
data.the-bad#The Bad:
Much of enterprise IT rests on technical foundations supplied by standards, platforms and vendors. Networking, virtualisation, identity and logging can often be treated as available services rather than systems to be designed. The work shifts towards selecting, configuring and combining established building blocks.
The same applies to business applications. HR, finance and customer management systems arrive with predefined workflows, data models and interfaces. Once a product has been selected, much of its architecture is already fixed. Integration becomes something fitted around it, with attention naturally turning to data mapping and synchronisation.
This encourages a habit of treating interfaces as implementation details, delegated to suppliers or integration teams. The question becomes whether systems can exchange data, rather than what each side must guarantee when they do. Buying the building blocks does not settle the responsibilities between them.
data.the-good#The Good:
Its strength is handling organisational complexity. It gives business and technology teams a common language and connects technology decisions to business purpose. Business architecture helps prevent individual systems and projects from being optimised at the expense of the whole.
By relating capabilities, processes, applications and ownership, it can reveal duplication, fragmented responsibilities and gaps that are difficult to see from within individual projects. It provides a basis for deciding where to invest, what to build or buy, and which systems to consolidate, modernise or retire. These decisions can then form a coordinated roadmap rather than a collection of unrelated initiatives.
data.the-problem#The problem:
Describing what must be true is not enough. “Protect sensitive data” and “ensure auditability” must become concrete obligations. Architecture must show where they are fulfilled, who is responsible and what evidence demonstrates fulfilment.
The full set of requirements applies to the system of systems as a whole. But passing that entire set to every subsystem does not solve the problem. Requirements must be broken down and deliberately allocated. Each subsystem must carry its share, with neither gaps between responsibilities nor unnecessary duplication.
Interfaces become contracts for the handover of responsibility. They specify what each side must fulfil, what it can rely on from the other, and how that handover can be verified. They are not merely connections for exchanging data, but boundaries for trust, control and verification. This is where an architecture focused on business processes and data models alone becomes too thin.
data.the-ugly#The Ugly:
Without clear interfaces and responsibility boundaries, compliance becomes difficult to prove. The architecture may describe the processes and applications involved, yet leave unanswered which requirements each subsystem must fulfil. Policy states what must be done, but does not establish where it is done or who must demonstrate it.
Requirements apply to the system of systems as a whole, but their fulfilment depends on deliberately allocated obligations across its subsystems. The architecture must establish how those obligations fit together.
Without explicit interface contracts, there is also no agreed basis for verifying the handover. What must the sending system guarantee? What must the receiving system check? Which evidence demonstrates that their combined behaviour fulfils the requirement? Individual systems may pass their assessments while the gaps between them remain both unspecified and untested.
data.what-is-business-architecture#What is Bu: Business architecture is concerned with how the enterprise works and how it should evolve. What capabilities does it need? Which processes, information and applications support them? Who owns what, and how should change be governed? Capability maps, process and information models, and roadmaps help describe the answers and guide change.

data.policy-based-micro-segmentation-on-pfsen:
Maintain your policy and sanity with less than 25 easy-to-read firewall rules on a single page.
October 2026 · 15 min read

data:
Sometimes we want to play with things without risking our entire setup. Micro-segmentation reduces the blast radius. But I struggled to find a spolution that made policy-first segmentation straightforward across wired devices, Wi-Fi, and VMs. I went with pfSense. It has the building blocks. The challenge is putting them together while keeping the policy manageable. Here is how I made it work.
So I unboxed my new router and got to work. How hard could it be?
Turns out pfSense had another point of view. And that we must think very carefully about the trinity of Identity, Policy, and Topology. Because pfSense will happily gravitate to a topology first approach.
data.action#Action:
Using the test program, send UDP packets using the sender’s assigned IP address.
./spooftest send
data.action-1#Action:
Using the test program, send UDP packets with a forged source IP. Choose an address belonging to another configured client subnet, preferably one associated with a device that has additional permissions.
sudo ./spooftest send
data.completing-the-firewall-rules#Completing:
For the example given here, the rule set becomes:
Inter- faces Protocol Source Destination Port Description Block Any IPv6 * * * Block anything IPv6 Block WAN IPv4 * * * Block anything initiating from WAN Block LAN1 IPv4 !LAN1 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block LAN2 IPv4 !LAN2 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block LAN3 IPv4 !LAN3 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block VLAN10 IPv4 !VLAN10 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block VLAN20 IPv4 !VLAN20 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block MUSIC_ BRIDGE IPv4 !MUSIC_BRIDGE subnets * * Anti spoofing Pass LAN1 IPv4 POL_MGMT This Firewall (self) MGMT_ ROUTER Allow management of pfSense from only this interface Pass LAN1 IPv4 POL_MGMT DEV_NAS MGMT_ NAS Allow management of NAS from only this interface Block Any IPv4 TCP / UDP * This Firewall (self) MGMT_ ROUTER Prevent re-enabling mgmt below Block Any IPv4 TCP / UDP * DEV_NAS MGMT_ NAS Prevent re-enabling mgmt below Pass Any IPv4 TCP / UDP HOME_SUBNETS This firewall (self) 53 Allow DNS Pass Any IPv4 UDP HOME_SUBNETS This firewall (self) 123 Allowed NTP Pass Any IPv4 UDP POL_SYSLOG DEV_VM_SYSLOG 514 Devices allowed to send syslog Pass Any IPv4 TCP / UDP POL_MUSIC_ SYSTEM POL_MUSIC_ SYSTEM MUSIC_ CTRL Allowed to engage in music playback Pass Any IPv4 TCP / UDP POL_UPDATE UPDATE_DEST 123, 443 Allow limited internet access for update Pass Any IPv4 TCP / UDP POL_INTERNET !RFC1918_NETS * Allow full internet access Block Any IPv4 POL_NO_LOGGING_ ON_BLOCK * * Silence chatty logs Block Any IPv4 !127.0.0.1 !127.0.0.1 * Block (and log) everything not explicitly allowed above The exact rules will depend on which services your network needs. My goal is to keep the ruleset small enough that the complete policy can still be understood at a glance. Having all rules in one place helps enormously. Since misconfiguration is probably one of the more likely ways to weaken the segmentation, readability is not just a convenience. It is a security feature.
data.conclusions#Conclusions:
These are the principles that made micro-segmentation on pfSense work for me. It takes careful topology design and quite a bit of discipline, but once implemented, I find it surprisingly easy to live with.
The approach has its limitations, particularly regarding device identity. But with those limitations understood and the necessary safeguards in place, I believe it provides a useful level of protection for many home networks and small offices.
Andreas Olsson
data.expected-results#Expected results: Packets arrive at the receiver. The temporary pass rule’s counters increase. The anti-spoofing rule’s packet counters do not increase due to the test traffic. No firewall logs are generated for the test traffic. This also establishes that the test tool and network path work correctly.
data.expected-results-1#Expected results: No packets arrive at the receiver. The anti-spoofing rule’s packet counters increase. Firewall logs show the blocked packets, including their forged source addresses and ingress interface. The temporary pass rule’s counters do not increase due to the test traffic. Note that a missing packet at the receiver is not sufficient evidence of successful filtering. The anti-spoofing rule’s counters and logs must confirm that the test traffic was actually blocked. If necessary, use packet capture to establish that the packets reached pfSense.
data.explicitly-block-unsolicited-inbound-tra:
Even though pfSense blocks inbound WAN traffic by default, I add an explicit rule - again to clarify intent and reduce my cognitive load.
Inter- faces Protocol Source Destination Port Description Block WAN IPv4 * * * Block anything initiating from WAN
data.explicitly-enable-management#Explicitly:
Managing should only be allowed through dedicated interfaces, to reduce the risk of a compromise.
Inter- faces Protocol Source Destination Port Description Pass LAN1 IPv4 POL_MGMT This Firewall (self) MGMT_ ROUTER Allow management of pfSense from only this interface Pass LAN1 IPv4 POL_MGMT DEV_NAS MGMT_ NAS Allow management of NAS from only this interface Block Any IPv4 TCP / UDP * This Firewall (self) MGMT_ ROUTER Prevent re-enabling mgmt below Block Any IPv4 TCP / UDP * DEV_NAS MGMT_ NAS Prevent re-enabling mgmt below My personal preference is to disable the anti-lockout option in pfSense and have an explicit rule, leaving one place to look.
data.firewall-states#Firewall States:
Since the design relies on interface boundaries to constrain identity, firewall states should also respect those boundaries. I use interface-bound states rather than floating states, so packets matching an existing connection cannot simply arrive through another interface.
Verify your setting of the State Policy option under System > Advanced on the Firewall & NAT tab.
data.home_subnets-and-rfc1918_nets#HOME_SUBNE:
HOME_SUBNETS contains the subnets assigned to my internal interfaces, whereas RFC1918_NETS contains all private IPv4 address ranges.
I define the alias RFC1918_NETS as:
192.168.0.0 / 16 172.16.0.0 / 12 10.0.0.0 / 8 These are the private IPv4 address ranges (RFC 1918). By excluding RFC1918_NETS as a destination in the Internet access rules, I prevent devices from using those permissions to access other private networks, including networks outside my own setup.
Note that this does not strictly limit traffic to the public Internet; other reserved address ranges and the firewall’s own addresses may need separate consideration.
data.identity#Identity:
For the purpose of this article, identity means an IPv4 address used in policy, associated with a device through a static DHCP mapping.
On each client-facing interface, the DHCP server of the router maps the device’s MAC address to its intended IP address. The same approach is used for physical as well as virtual interfaces (VLANs). Note that this provides consistent addressing, but not authentication.
To protect against impersonation, we must use topology (i.e. which devices connect through which interfaces) and firewall rules.
data.inspecting-the-generated-rules#Inspectin:
pfSense translates its configuration into rules for the underlying packet filter (PF). In addition to our floating rules, pfSense generates automatic firewall and NAT rules.
Some of these are evaluated before our floating rules, potentially allowing traffic that our policy would otherwise block. We therefore need to inspect the effective ruleset, paying particular attention to NAT and automatically generated permissions.
From the pfSense shell, run:
Command Explanation pfctl -sr Show the effective firewall rules pfctl -sn Show the effective NAT rules pfSsh.php playback pfanchordrill Show additional rules in PF anchors We are particularly interested in:
Unexpected pass rules: Check for automatically generated permissions that could bypass our floating rules. NAT port forwards: Look for unexpected redirects, particularly rdr pass, which can permit traffic without a separate firewall pass rule. Dynamic rules: Check for rules created by services or packages, such as UPnP IGD/PCP. Ordinary outbound NAT rules are expected, since they allow our internal devices to share the WAN address. They do not, by themselves, grant permission to initiate connections.
The goal is not to audit every internal rule generated by pfSense, but to establish that no unexpected permissions undermine our segmentation policy.
See also the Netgate documentation: Ordering of NAT and Firewall Processing
data.my-setup#My setup: Router: Netgate 6100 (pfSense+) WiFi: Ubiquiti wireless access point NAS: Synology (running a handful of Virtual Machines) Half a dozen physical computers (many over Wi-Fi) Local AI server A legacy music system using UPnP Note that I do not use a switch. This is what makes micro-segmentation possible without having to configure VLANs for everything. More on this later.
data.no-ipv6#No IPv6:
The design is based on IPv4. Rather than accidentally leaving an unsegmented IPv6 path, I disable the allow IPv6 option under System → Advanced → Networking. I also add an explicit rule to clarify intent and reduce cognitive load for myself.
Inter- faces Protocol Source Destination Port Description Block Any IPv6 * * * Block anything IPv6
data.note-do-not-accidentally-block-pfsense-i:
There is one wrinkle when using floating rules on Any: Any also includes the loopback interface (lo0). pfSense uses loopback internally; for example, by default the firewall itself uses the DNS resolver at 127.0.0.1. Although pfSense generates rules to allow loopback traffic, these IPv4 rules are not quick, so a later user-defined quick catch-all block can override them. The catch-all policy block should therefore either exclude loopback traffic or, preferably, only apply to the network interfaces covered by the policy.
In this example I have baked the necessary exception for loopback into the blocking rule itself. This is more permissive than strictly necessary. On the other hand, it saves screen space and is easy to live with, as new interfaces are automatically included in the catch-all rule.
data.policy#Policy:
Policy membership is implemented with nested aliases on three levels:
Device Group Policy Where the policy level is used in the firewall rules. This makes the rules readable and easy to understand.

Limited ports and IP addresses A few notes:

data.preparation#Preparation:
The tests require two devices on different network segments: a sender and a receiver. A small test program repeatedly sends UDP packets to the receiver, for some tests using a spoofed source IP address.
To isolate the anti-spoofing mechanism from the ordinary communication policy, add a temporary floating pass rule immediately after the anti-spoofing rules but before the normal policy rules:
Setting Value Action Pass Interface Sender’s interface Direction In Quick Enabled Protocol IPv4 UDP Source Any Destination Receiver’s IP address Destination port 39000 Logging Disabled This allows test packets to reach the receiver, provided they have not already been blocked by the anti-spoofing rules.
Before testing:
Make sure logging is enabled on the anti-spoofing rule(s). Compile the test program. It is available as a downloadable C source file . cc -std=c11 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic spooftest.c -o spooftest Start the receiver, listening on UDP port 39000. Ensure its local firewall permits the traffic. ./spooftest receive Open the pfSense firewall logs and rule counters to observe the results. The sender, when started, will repeatedly send traffic using a new UDP source port for each packet to avoid reusing existing firewall states.
Make sure the temporary pass rule is reached by the test traffic and that no existing firewall states interfere with the tests.
data.protect-against-spoofing-of-ip-addresses:
To support micro-segmentation we need a sufficiently trustworthy identity, because if a device can impersonate another identity it may inherit that device’s privileges.
A device can choose its own MAC address and source IP address. The design therefore cannot trust the address merely because DHCP assigned it. For each routed client interface, I explicitly block packets whose source address does not belong to the subnet permitted on that interface.
This effectively locks the device to the address range permitted on its interface. If that interface serves only one device, the topology gives us a much stronger identity boundary.
Inter- faces Protocol Source Destination Port Description Block LAN1 IPv4 !LAN1 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block LAN2 IPv4 !LAN2 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block LAN3 IPv4 !LAN3 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block VLAN10 IPv4 !VLAN10 subnets * * Anti spoofing Block VLAN20 IPv4 !VLAN20 subnets * * Anti spoofing Note that this restricts devices to their assigned subnets, not to individual DHCP addresses. Addresses within the same subnet must therefore be considered interchangeable from a security perspective.
These rules should have logging enabled. A match indicates either a misconfiguration or a possible attempt at IP spoofing. Both are worth investigating.
Unfortunately, this adds some unavoidable topology-specific bulk to the top of the ruleset. The important part is that it remains isolated from the policy rules below, so the policy itself stays readable.
When adding a new interface, remember to add its source-address restriction before enabling the corresponding policy permissions.
data.security-rules---bottom-set#Security Rul:
The bottom security rule set has one main purpose: block everything not explicitly allowed by the policy rules above.
Inter- faces Protocol Source Destination Port Description Block Any IPv4 POL_NO_LOGGING_ ON_BLOCK * * Silence chatty logs Block Any IPv4 !127.0.0.1 !127.0.0.1 * Block (and log) everything not explicitly allowed above The first rule suppresses logging for known noisy traffic that is already intentionally blocked.
Logging should be enabled on the final catch-all rule. Any match means traffic occurred that was not accounted for by the policy rules above. These logs are useful both during tuning and for later monitoring.
data.security-rules---top-set#Security Rules: Before evaluating the communication policy, I use a small set of security rules to establish the assumptions the design depends on. These rules are placed above the policy rules.
data.tear-down#Tear Down:
After testing, remove the temporary pass rule and clear any states it created. Remove test program and binary.
Repeat both tests for the different types of interfaces: physical, virtual and bridge.
data.the-bridge-and-legacy-music-system#The B:
The bridge acts much like a switch with several interfaces for the same subnet.
For this design, filtering is performed on the logical bridge interface rather than on its individual member interfaces. This requires the following two tunables:
Tunable name Description Value net.link.bridge.pfil_member Packet filter on the member interface 0 net.link.bridge.pfil_bridge Packet filter on the bridge interface 1 Devices sharing the bridge can impersonate each other’s IP addresses. However, firewall filtering still limits which services (ports) can be reached from within the subnet of the bridge. In particular, access to the NAS management interface on ports 5000–5001 is not permitted, and management is done from an interface (LAN1) outside the bridge itself.
The reason for the bridge is to cater for a legacy music system that uses UPnP.
It is important to distinguish between UPnP discovery and control, used by my music system, and UPnP IGD/PCP, which can allow devices to request dynamic port mappings on the router. The latter is known for its security issues and I recommend to keep it disabled.
Also, to keep the rule set manageable I include 239.255.255.250 in POL_MUSIC_SYSTEM and 1900 as well as 80 and 49152:65535 in the MUSIC_CTRL port alias. This makes the rule less restrictive than strictly necessary and leaves other services within that range reachable. But I consider these devices reasonably trustworthy. And for me, the additional risk is acceptable.
data.topology#Topology:
The topology must support both identity and policy. For this, two things are required:
Devices that need to be separated from each other must be placed on different routed interfaces or VLANs (to enforce identity) Traffic between devices that needs to be separated must cross the firewall (to enforce policy) Fortunately, for separate routed interfaces and VLANs, 1) also gives us 2): traffic between them must cross pfSense.
In my setup there are four distinct scenarios:
Physical devices that connect directly to the router. One device for one interface. Virtual machines that connect through VLANs. Here I use the virtual switch in the NAS to configure VLAN tags for the VMs. The Wi-Fi access point is configured with different virtual access points where each SSID is mapped to a different VLAN. For the legacy music system I use a bridge across a number of interfaces. The bridge forms one logical Layer-2 segment, acting much like a switch. Traffic can still be filtered by pfSense, but devices within the bridge no longer get strong identity separation from topology. Note that not all VMs get an individual VLAN. For example the syslog collector and Elastic server (a simple SIEM) live on the same VLAN as they are both part of the same function. This is why there is no firewall rule between the collector and the SIEM: the communication between them stays in the virtual switch and is not subject to the router’s firewall.
Effectively, I trust these three components to preserve the segmentation:
pfSense, for routing and firewall enforcement the NAS virtual switch, for VM VLAN assignment the Wi-Fi AP, for wireless VLAN assignment Plus the computer I use to administer the other three.
A compromise or misconfiguration of any of these could weaken or bypass the segmentation.
data.using-floating-rules#Using Floating Rule:
The design uses floating rules exclusively. This keeps the complete ruleset on a single page, which makes it easier to review as one policy. To make evaluation predictable, all rules are defined as:
Inbound Quick
data.verifying-the-design#Verifying the Desig:
To verify the design, we need to perform a few targeted checks. I use two approaches:
Inspecting the rules that pfSense generates for the underlying packet filter (PF), particularly those related to NAT. Testing that the anti-spoofing rules behave as intended and generate the expected logs. This is not a penetration test, nor is the goal to verify the full functionality of pfSense. But we do need to establish that the assumptions our design depends on hold in practice.
Fortunately, this requires only a few targeted tests. For the anti-spoofing rules, we can use a single temporary, narrowly scoped pass rule to isolate the behaviour we want to verify and a simple test program for sending and receiving traffic.
data.why-it-works-and-what-must-be-true#Why i: There are a number of things that must be configured correctly for the design to work as intended. Most of these are expressed in the firewall rules, either in the top or bottom set of security rules.
